# Implement block: Island Toast Stack (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Island Toast Stack" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

An original Native Cook design on a dark lock screen: a deep ink wallpaper with wide, soft pools of cobalt, plum and teal, and a date, a big white rounded 9:41 and a hint line at the bottom. A black pill sits exactly over the Dynamic Island (126 × 37 pt; just under the notch on older iPhones; Android keeps its status bar and shows the pill just under it only while something grows out of it) and morphs into live toasts: an incoming call from Theo Marsh with red and green round buttons, a message from Rafael Ortiz, an upload of 24 photos to "Lisbon, spring" with a blue progress ring, and a "Sourdough proof" kitchen timer in large orange rounded digits. Each toast is the island grown to the screen width minus 20 pt and 99 pt tall with continuous corners. After a moment it drops out of the island as a black card into a stack below, joined by a gooey neck that thins and snaps, and clears into the system’s notification material: the wallpaper seen through the card under a grey tint, with older cards peeking out as narrower, darker bottom edges. Each card reads like an iOS notification: a 38 pt icon (an app squircle, or the contact’s photo with an app badge), a semibold title with "now", and a line or two: "Missed call · mobile", the message, "Uploading 16 of 24 photos", the timer’s orange countdown "left · Kitchen". Tapping the stack opens it into a list under a "Notifications" header with a Show less pill and a round ✕ that clears it; a card swiped sideways is thrown away. Tapping the island brings the next toast, pulling it down (also from just under it, out of reach of the system’s top-edge swipe) opens the timer as a big card with Pause and +5 min that pushes the stack down, and clearing draws every card back up into the island while it gulps each one.

**Motion.** The island morphs out of its own frame on springs, width a little ahead of height (width 520 ms at damping ratio 0.7, height 600 ms at 0.74), corners kept continuous with a radius of min(44 pt, half the height); it closes on a calmer spring (500 ms, 0.86). Content fades in only once the shape has settled: after 210 ms, over 240 ms (ease-out 0.23, 1, 0.32, 1), lifting 6 pt and growing from 96%. After 1.9 s the content fades out in 110 ms, the island closes, and the toast's card is drawn from the open toast's frame down into the front slot on a spring (680 ms, 0.76) while the island shrinks back: while they overlap, concave 9 pt fillets round the corners where island and card meet; once apart, a neck leaves the island's bottom edge and lands tangentially on the card's top edge, its waist pinching (to 82% × (1 − gap/24)^1.3 of the anchor) and flaring 35% of the gap onto the card, snapping at a 24 pt gap. Closed, the stack sits 12 pt below the island; cards are 80 pt tall with 22 pt continuous corners, and each card behind the front is 11 pt narrower on either side and shows 9 pt lower (the second 9 pt, the third 18 pt, no further). A card is the island's black while it leaves (so the neck reads as one shape) and clears into the notification material between 50% and 90% of its arrival: the wallpaper seen through the card’s shape (it stays put on screen while a swipe turns the card) under a grey fill of rgba(128, 128, 138, 0.4), with black over the cards behind at 38% × their depth, so each one back is darker; the third card back melts away as it slides further back; cards move between slots on a 480 ms, 0.84 spring. Tapping the stack opens it on a 520 ms, 0.82 spring into a list 88 pt apart under a 46 pt header that fades and slides in 10 pt; its ✕ clears the stack the same way the demo does. A card follows a sideways drag with a slight turn (0.035° per pt) and fades; released past 32% of the width or faster than 900 pt/s it flies off with the finger's velocity (380 ms, critically damped, clamped) and the rest close up, otherwise it springs back (420 ms, 0.72). The island sits inside the system's top-edge swipe (Notification Center, the Android shade), so a pull also starts in a 108 pt band under the closed island, toast-wide, once the finger has gone 10 pt down (a sideways move of 16 pt leaves it to the cards), and a downward drag of 12 pt on the closed stack's front card hands the touch to the same pull; a tap in that band counts as a tap on the island. Pulling the island down opens it with the finger over 170 pt (width leading 1.6× the height), past which it stretches on a tanh band; a release past 42% or a downward flick over 600 pt/s opens the 228 pt big card carrying the release speed, otherwise it closes; the stack is pushed down by the island's extra height. Clearing raises the cards into the island one by one, 120 ms apart, each over 460 ms (ease-in-out 0.77, 0, 0.175, 1) darkening from the material back to black in the first 40% of the way, and the island gulps each with an underdamped spring kick (420 ms, ratio 0.45, 320 pt/s). The upload ring fills linearly over 9 s; the timer, count and percentage are read from the clock. Light haptics mark a toast called up by hand and a card thrown away, a medium one the big card. The self-playing demo loops every 16 s (LOOP = 16): the call at 0.6 s, the message at 3.0 s, the upload at 5.4 s and the timer at 7.8 s, the stack opens at 10.3 s, the message is thrown away at 11.4 s, the stack closes at 12.3 s, the big card opens at 12.9 s and closes at 14.2 s, everything is drawn back into the island from 14.7 s, at rest before the loop ends. A touch pauses it for 4 s, then everything settles back into the island and it starts over 1.2 s later. Under reduced motion the island changes size on a 220 ms ease-out with no overshoot, there is no neck, cards fade in place, content does not lift or scale, and thrown-away cards just disappear.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [IslandToastStackDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Modals/IslandToastStack/IslandToastStackDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [IslandToastStack.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Modals/IslandToastStack/IslandToastStack.swift)
- [IslandToastStackEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Modals/IslandToastStack/IslandToastStackEngine.swift)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
